items.stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes heavily reports several months of difficulty rising from chairs, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Examination shows proximal leg weakness with absent knee reflexes that briefly return after 10 seconds of maximal quadriceps contraction. Which antibody is most likely to be found?
items.explanation: Proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and reflexes that facilitate after exercise describe Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is paraneoplastic in most smokers because of small cell lung cancer. Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q type calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release. Acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies cause postsynaptic myasthenia gravis with fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness and preserved reflexes. Potassium channel complex antibodies produce neuromyotonia or limbic encephalitis.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman reports morning jerks of both arms that make her drop her coffee cup, and one generalized convulsion after a night of sleep deprivation. Electroencephalography shows 4 to 6 Hz generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges. She plans to become pregnant within a year. Which maintenance medication is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy needs a broad-spectrum agent. Valproate is highly effective but carries a high risk of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm, so it is avoided in women who may conceive. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers that can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures. Levetiracetam or lamotrigine controls generalized seizure types with a lower teratogenic risk.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking an oral contraceptive has 3 days of worsening headache followed by a focal seizure of the left arm and mild left hand weakness. Computed tomography shows a small right parasagittal hemorrhagic infarct. Which study is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance venography of the head
Conventional catheter angiography of the carotid arteries
Transcranial Doppler of the middle cerebral arteries
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure only
items.explanation: Headache, seizure, and a venous-pattern hemorrhagic infarct in a woman using estrogen suggest cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, best shown by magnetic resonance or computed tomography venography. Arterial studies such as carotid catheter angiography and transcranial Doppler assess arteries and would miss sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture adds little diagnostically and carries risk when imaging shows a mass effect or hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease has recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of children in the house and delusions of spousal infidelity. Cognition is otherwise intact, and he takes carbidopa-levodopa and pramipexole. After pramipexole is reduced, symptoms persist. Which antipsychotic is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Parkinson disease psychosis that persists after dopaminergic simplification is best treated with a serotonin 5-HT2A inverse agonist such as pimavanserin, which does not block dopamine receptors. Low-dose quetiapine and clozapine are alternatives. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine antagonize D2 receptors and worsen motor function, and conventional agents risk severe rigidity, falls, and prolonged immobility in these patients.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops fever, then drowsiness, ataxia, and right hemiparesis 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. Magnetic resonance imaging shows large asymmetric white matter lesions in both hemispheres and the thalamus. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Oral prednisone at a low dose for 1 week
items.explanation: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a monophasic, postinfectious demyelinating illness with encephalopathy and multifocal deficits, and the first-line treatment is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids for 3 to 5 days. Acyclovir alone treats herpes encephalitis, which would be focal and temporal. Interferon beta is a long-term therapy for relapsing multiple sclerosis. Low-dose oral prednisone is inadequate for severe disease.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has 1 year of a slow, magnetic gait, followed by urinary urgency and mild forgetfulness. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Which finding best predicts benefit from a shunt?
options: Gait speed improvement after a lumbar tap
Elevated opening pressure above 25 cm of water
items.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, urinary urgency, and cognitive slowing. A measurable improvement in gait after removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid predicts a good shunt response. Marked dementia predicts a poor result, and opening pressure is normal in this condition by definition. White matter changes occur in many older adults and do not predict response.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has a 2-year history of intention tremor and gait ataxia. His grandson has autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. Magnetic resonance imaging shows middle cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity. Which mechanism most likely explains his illness?
options: Premutation CGG repeat expansion in FMR1
Full mutation CAG expansion in ATXN1
Trinucleotide expansion in the frataxin gene
items.explanation: Fragile X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome occurs in older carriers of an FMR1 premutation of 55 to 200 CGG repeats, and a grandchild with a full mutation of more than 200 repeats has fragile X syndrome. Middle cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity is a typical imaging marker. ATXN1 expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, 15q deletion causes Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome, and frataxin expansion causes Friedreich ataxia in the young.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on a stable dose of lithium starts a new antihypertensive and develops coarse tremor, ataxia, and vomiting 5 days later. Which newly started drug most likely caused her lithium level to rise?
items.explanation: Thiazide diuretics increase proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium and can raise serum levels by 25 to 40 percent, producing coarse tremor, ataxia, and gastrointestinal upset. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs act similarly. Amlodipine, acetaminophen, and omeprazole do not meaningfully alter renal lithium clearance, so they would not explain the toxicity, so levels should still be rechecked after any new prescription.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has attacks of severe right orbital pain lasting 60 minutes with tearing, nasal congestion, and restlessness, occurring nightly for 5 weeks. He asks about a preventive drug. Which is the best option, and what should be checked beforehand?
options: Sumatriptan daily, after liver function tests
Propranolol, after a pulmonary function test
items.explanation: Cluster headache prevention begins with verapamil, and the electrocardiogram checks the PR interval because heart block can occur at the high doses required. Sumatriptan is an acute treatment, with oxygen, and is not a daily preventive. Propranolol and amitriptyline are used in migraine and have little evidence in cluster headache. Oxygen at 12 to 15 liters per minute remains the key acute therapy.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden knee buckling when laughing. A multiple sleep latency test the morning after a normal overnight study shows a mean latency of 4 minutes. Which additional finding confirms narcolepsy type 1?
options: Persistent slow wave sleep during naps
Obstructive apneas on the preceding study
items.explanation: Narcolepsy is diagnosed when the mean sleep latency is 8 minutes or less with 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods, including the one on the preceding night if present. Cataplexy defines type 1 clinically, and low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin also confirms it. Slow wave sleep during naps, obstructive apneas, and periodic limb movements do not define narcolepsy.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with severe vomiting from hyperemesis gravidarum for 6 weeks has confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and a wide-based gait. Her glucose is 62 mg/dL, and intravenous dextrose is available. What should be given first?
options: Intravenous dextrose alone, followed by thiamine later
Oral multivitamin once she can swallow
Intravenous thiamine before or with the dextrose
items.explanation: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia indicate Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency due to prolonged vomiting and poor nutrition. Glucose given before thiamine can consume remaining thiamine cofactor stores and precipitate worsening, so thiamine is given first or together. Oral supplementation is poorly absorbed, and magnesium is a cofactor but does not replace thiamine. Delay risks permanent amnestic Korsakoff syndrome.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has an unsteady gait, lightning pains in the legs, and small irregular pupils that constrict on near focus but not to light. Serum treponemal antibody testing is reactive and cerebrospinal fluid is abnormal. Which is the recommended treatment?
options: Single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin
Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days
items.explanation: Argyll Robertson pupils and tabes dorsalis indicate neurosyphilis, which requires intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days because benzathine penicillin does not reliably reach the cerebrospinal fluid. Short courses of doxycycline or ceftriaxone are alternatives only in selected penicillin-allergic patients and are not preferred. Follow-up cerebrospinal fluid testing assesses response, and HIV testing is advised for all patients with syphilis.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends his neck. He now has burning pain in both hands, marked bilateral arm weakness, and milder leg weakness. Which pattern of injury is most likely?
options: Anterior cord syndrome with loss of pain below the injury
Brown-Sequard syndrome with ipsilateral proprioceptive loss
Posterior cord syndrome with loss of vibration only
Central cord syndrome with greater arm weakness
items.explanation: Hyperextension of a stenotic cervical canal damages the central gray matter and the medial corticospinal fibers to the arms, which are more medially placed than leg fibers, so arm weakness exceeds leg weakness with variable sensory loss. Anterior cord injury spares dorsal columns, Brown-Sequard causes a hemisection pattern, and an isolated posterior cord lesion is rare and does not cause marked weakness.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has horizontal diplopia on looking to the left. On leftward gaze, the right eye fails to adduct, and the left eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is intact. Where is the lesion?
items.explanation: Failure of adduction of one eye on contralateral gaze with nystagmus in the abducting eye and preserved convergence is an internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The lesion is in the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the side of the eye that fails to adduct, here the right, and demyelination is a leading cause in young women. A lesion of the abducens nucleus causes a conjugate gaze palsy, and nerve lesions would impair convergence.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has a newly diagnosed ring-enhancing frontal mass, and biopsy shows IDH wild-type glioblastoma. His performance status is good after surgery. What is standard care after maximal safe resection?
options: Whole brain radiation followed by observation
items.explanation: The standard of care for glioblastoma in patients with good functional status is maximal safe resection followed by focal radiation with concurrent temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide cycles. This improves survival compared with radiation alone. Whole brain radiation is used for multiple metastases, and chemotherapy alone is inferior and reserved for patients unfit for radiation, such as frail older adults.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has right leg weakness and loss of vibration and position sense in the right leg, together with loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg and trunk up to the level of the umbilicus. Where is the lesion?
options: Right hemicord at the thoracic level
Left hemicord at the thoracic level
Right dorsal columns at the cervical level
Central cord at the lumbar level
items.explanation: A hemisection of the cord, Brown-Sequard syndrome, produces ipsilateral weakness and loss of dorsal column function because those pathways cross high in the medulla, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature because spinothalamic fibers cross within a segment or two of entry. The signs are on the right for weakness and vibration, so the lesion is right sided at a thoracic level. A left lesion would reverse the pattern, and central cord lesions produce a bilateral suspended pattern.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has 2 weeks of psychosis, then seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and a decreased level of consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and magnetic resonance imaging is normal. Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are present in the spinal fluid. Which study should be performed next?
options: Pelvic imaging for an ovarian teratoma
items.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis frequently presents in young women with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias, and autonomic instability, and many have an ovarian teratoma. Tumor detection and removal improves outcome, so pelvic imaging should follow antibody confirmation along with immunotherapy. Bone scans, prion protein testing, and carotid imaging do not address the underlying paraneoplastic trigger or the treatable tumor.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease has dizziness on standing. Supine blood pressure is 168/96 mm Hg and falls to 110/64 mm Hg after 3 minutes upright without a rise in heart rate. Which strategy is most appropriate at night?
options: Give fludrocortisone at bedtime to raise volume
Elevate the head of the bed 30 degrees
items.explanation: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension often coexists with supine hypertension because of a failed baroreflex. Raising the head of the bed by about 30 degrees reduces nocturnal pressure and natriuresis. Pressor drugs such as midodrine and fludrocortisone aggravate nighttime hypertension and should be taken in the daytime, with the last dose several hours before bed. Added salt worsens supine pressure as well.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has had progressive symmetric weakness of both arms and legs with numbness for 14 weeks. Reflexes are absent, and nerve conduction studies show multifocal conduction block with prolonged distal latencies. Which feature most strongly separates her diagnosis from Guillain-Barre syndrome?
options: Progression continuing for more than 8 weeks
Elevated protein with normal cell count in cerebrospinal fluid
Symmetric involvement of proximal and distal muscles
items.explanation: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy is defined by progression, or relapses, beyond 8 weeks, whereas Guillain-Barre syndrome reaches its nadir within 4 weeks. Areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation, and symmetric proximal and distal weakness occur in both disorders, so they cannot discriminate. The time course therefore guides the diagnosis and leads to treatment with immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, or plasma exchange rather than supportive care alone.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man is found convulsing in a parking lot, and paramedics have no intravenous access after 5 minutes of continuous seizure activity. Which is the best immediate treatment?
options: Oral lorazepam tablets placed under the tongue
items.explanation: Benzodiazepines are the first-line therapy for status epilepticus, and intramuscular midazolam is as effective as intravenous lorazepam when access is absent. Levetiracetam and phenytoin are second-line agents given after a benzodiazepine, and phenytoin takes time to infuse and requires cardiac monitoring. An actively convulsing patient cannot safely take sublingual or oral tablets, and absorption would be unreliable.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes develops sudden vertigo, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right face and the left body, right ptosis with miosis, and right limb ataxia. Which additional finding is expected with this lesion?
options: Contralateral hemiparesis of the face, arm, and leg
Bilateral loss of vibration sense in the legs
Ipsilateral loss of the gag reflex
items.explanation: Crossed sensory loss, Horner syndrome, dysphagia, and ataxia define lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion. Involvement of the nucleus ambiguus causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and an impaired ipsilateral gag. The pyramids lie medially and are spared, so hemiparesis is absent. Vibration is carried in the medial lemniscus, and a field defect would signal a posterior cerebral lesion.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has progressive chorea and irritability. His father died in an institution at 55. Genetic testing shows 43 CAG repeats in the HTT gene. His father had 41 repeats and an onset at 52. Which phenomenon explains the earlier onset in the son?
options: Genomic imprinting of the maternal allele
X-linked dominant inheritance with variable penetrance
items.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder, and repeat length correlates inversely with age at onset. The CAG tract is unstable and tends to expand when passed through the male germline, producing earlier onset in successive generations, called anticipation. Imprinting, mitochondrial heteroplasmy, and X-linked inheritance do not describe the pattern of the HTT gene on chromosome 4.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had an episode of optic neuritis and now presents with new left leg numbness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows several periventricular lesions, one of which enhances, and two that do not. Which statement best describes her imaging?
options: It fails dissemination in time without a repeat scan
It shows dissemination in time by mixed lesion ages
It excludes multiple sclerosis because enhancement is present
It requires oligoclonal bands to show dissemination in space
items.explanation: The McDonald criteria allow dissemination in time to be shown on a single scan when an asymptomatic enhancing lesion and a nonenhancing lesion coexist, indicating lesions of different ages. Repeat imaging is therefore unnecessary here. Enhancement is typical of acute demyelination and does not exclude it. Oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time, not for dissemination in space, which is shown by lesions in separate regions.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has well-formed visual hallucinations of small animals, day-to-day fluctuating alertness, and acting out of dreams for several years. Mild parkinsonism developed after cognitive decline. Which treatment is the best initial option for her cognitive symptoms?
items.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by fluctuations, visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement behavior disorder, and parkinsonism. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine improve cognition and often reduce hallucinations. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol can cause severe sensitivity reactions. Memantine has modest benefit but is not the best first choice, and anticholinergics counteract cholinesterase inhibitors and worsen cognition.

items.stem: A 3-year-old girl who walked and spoke single words at 12 months has lost purposeful hand use, develops constant midline hand wringing, and has episodes of breath holding. Head growth has decelerated. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Regression of acquired skills with loss of hand function, stereotyped hand wringing, breathing irregularities, and deceleration of head growth after apparently normal early development describe Rett syndrome in girls, caused by mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene. FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome, UBE3A deficiency causes Angelman syndrome with a happy demeanor and ataxia, and SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man starts linezolid while taking sertraline and develops agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and a temperature of 39 C. Which finding best distinguishes his illness from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
items.explanation: Serotonin syndrome typically has rapid onset after a serotonergic exposure and features clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, mydriasis, and diarrhea. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days to weeks after dopamine antagonist exposure and shows lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia. Elevated creatine kinase and fever occur in both conditions, so they cannot separate them. Early recognition and stopping the offending drug are essential for recovery.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has brief electric shock-like pains in the right cheek triggered by chewing and brushing her teeth. Examination is normal, and magnetic resonance imaging shows a vascular loop contacting the trigeminal root. Which drug is first-line?
items.explanation: Classic trigeminal neuralgia from neurovascular compression responds best to carbamazepine, a sodium channel blocker, and a rapid response supports the diagnosis. Lamotrigine, gabapentin, and baclofen are second-line or adjunctive. Microvascular decompression is considered when medication fails or is not tolerated. Because response is often dramatic, a failed trial of this drug should prompt a review of the diagnosis. Dosing is titrated slowly, and sodium and blood counts are monitored for adverse effects.

items.stem: A woman of 45 describes creeping leg sensations at bedtime that ease only when she paces. Ferritin is 28 ng/mL. After 18 months of pramipexole, symptoms now start at midday and have spread to her arms. What is the best next step?
options: Increase the pramipexole dose and add ropinirole
Replace iron and use an alpha-2-delta ligand
items.explanation: Restless legs syndrome treated with dopamine agonists can develop augmentation, with earlier onset and spread of symptoms, and raising the dose worsens it. Iron should be replaced when ferritin is below about 75 ng/mL, and an alpha-2-delta ligand such as gabapentin or pregabalin is the preferred alternative. Opioids are reserved for refractory cases, and antihistamines worsen restless legs.

items.stem: A 66-year-old vegan man has 6 months of numb feet, unsteady gait, and a spastic leg weakness with absent ankle reflexes. Vibration sense is lost in the toes, and he has macrocytic anemia. Which laboratory pair is most helpful when serum vitamin B12 is borderline?
options: Low folate with normal homocysteine and low iron
items.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency affects the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts, and peripheral nerves. When serum levels are borderline, elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm functional deficiency. Low folate raises homocysteine without methylmalonic acid, mitochondrial disease raises lactate, and copper deficiency can mimic the myelopathy but is identified by low copper levels. Treatment is parenteral replacement of vitamin B12.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection has 2 weeks of headache and confusion. India ink is positive, and the lumbar puncture opening pressure is 38 cm of water. Besides induction antifungal therapy, what should be done for the pressure?
options: Place a lumbar drain only after 4 weeks
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis often causes elevated intracranial pressure, and removing cerebrospinal fluid until closing pressure is below 20 cm of water, repeated as needed, reduces morbidity and mortality. Acetazolamide is not effective in this setting and may cause acidosis. Corticosteroids worsen outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis. A lumbar drain is reserved for refractory cases and not delayed for weeks.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with severe cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends his neck. He has no fracture. He now has burning hands and arm weakness greater than leg weakness, with urinary retention and variable sensory loss below the neck. Which syndrome is this?
items.explanation: Hyperextension in a spondylotic canal injures the central cervical cord, where the corticospinal fibers to the arms lie more medially. The arms are therefore weaker than the legs, with bladder dysfunction and a variable sensory loss. Anterior cord injury spares dorsal column function and causes loss of motor and pain sensation below the lesion. Brown-Sequard gives ipsilateral weakness with contralateral pain loss, and posterior cord injury mainly impairs proprioception.

items.stem: Shortly after a viral illness, a 34-year-old teacher is told her left pupil is larger in bright light. It reacts very slowly to light but constricts slowly with prolonged near effort. Her left knee and ankle reflexes are absent. Which drop test confirms the diagnosis?
options: Apraclonidine causing dilation of the large pupil
Cocaine failing to dilate the small pupil
Dilute pilocarpine constricting the large pupil
items.explanation: A tonic pupil with light-near dissociation and diminished tendon reflexes is Adie syndrome, resulting from damage to the ciliary ganglion with aberrant regeneration. Denervation supersensitivity makes the pupil constrict to dilute pilocarpine, which normal pupils do not. Apraclonidine, cocaine, and hydroxyamphetamine are used to confirm and localize Horner syndrome, in which the abnormal pupil is small, not large.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has 3 weeks of confusion and personality change. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a single homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum. He is HIV negative. Before biopsy, which medication should be avoided if possible?
items.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass in an immunocompetent patient suggests primary central nervous system lymphoma. Steroids are lympholytic and can shrink the tumor and cause nondiagnostic biopsy specimens, so they should be withheld unless herniation threatens. Antiseizure drugs such as levetiracetam, analgesics, and antiemetics do not affect histology. High-dose methotrexate is the backbone of treatment after tissue diagnosis.

items.stem: A 59-year-old right-handed man has an infarct involving the left angular gyrus. Which set of findings is expected?
options: Left neglect, anosognosia, and constructional apraxia
Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right-left confusion
Pure word deafness and normal reading
items.explanation: Dominant hemisphere angular gyrus damage causes Gerstmann syndrome, consisting of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right-left disorientation. Neglect with anosognosia and constructional difficulty follows non-dominant parietal injury. Prosopagnosia and color loss reflect ventral occipitotemporal lesions. Pure word deafness arises from bilateral or dominant superior temporal lesions that disconnect auditory input from language areas, which is a separate syndrome.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has 3 weeks of brief arm and facial jerks occurring dozens of times a day, followed by amnesia and confusion. Serum sodium is 126 mmol/L. Magnetic resonance imaging shows right medial temporal hyperintensity. Which antibody is most likely?
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatremia, and limbic encephalitis in an older man are characteristic of anti-LGI1 encephalitis. It usually responds well to immunotherapy, and early treatment of the seizures may prevent cognitive decline. Glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies are linked to stiff person syndrome and cerebellar ataxia, amphiphysin to paraneoplastic stiff person syndrome, and aquaporin-4 to neuromyelitis optica.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has 2 years of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and now wakes with morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and forced vital capacity falls by 30 percent when he lies supine. Muscle biopsy shows vacuoles with glycogen accumulation. Which treatment is indicated?
options: High-carbohydrate diet loading before each exertion
items.explanation: Proximal myopathy with early diaphragm involvement, a supine fall in vital capacity, and glycogen-filled vacuoles indicates late-onset Pompe disease, an acid maltase deficiency. Enzyme replacement slows decline in motor and respiratory function. Prednisone and immunoglobulin treat inflammatory myopathies, which do not show glycogen vacuoles. Carbohydrate loading helps disorders such as McArdle disease only in the sense of exercise tolerance and does not correct a lysosomal enzyme defect.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred because she stares and stops talking for about 10 seconds, dozens of times daily, and her grades are falling. Hyperventilation for 3 minutes reproduces an event, and electroencephalography shows 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges. No convulsions have been witnessed. Which agent should be started first?
items.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy responds well to ethosuximide, which blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and is the first choice when no generalized tonic-clonic seizures exist. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can worsen absence seizures. Gabapentin has little efficacy in generalized epilepsy. Valproate is an alternative but is reserved for patients who also have convulsive seizures because of its toxicity profile.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman arrives 90 minutes after sudden right arm weakness and aphasia. Her blood pressure is 198/112 mmHg, and head computed tomography shows no hemorrhage. She meets all other criteria for thrombolysis. What should be done about her blood pressure?
options: Lower it below 185/110 mmHg before giving alteplase
Withhold alteplase because any pressure above 160 mmHg excludes treatment
Give alteplase now and treat pressure afterward
Lower it below 140/90 mmHg before giving alteplase
items.explanation: Thrombolysis is safe only when pressure is under 185 systolic and 110 diastolic before the infusion and under 180/105 for the 24 hours afterward. Rapidly acting intravenous agents such as labetalol or nicardipine achieve this. Treating after the bolus ignores the hemorrhage risk, withholding treatment at 160 is overly restrictive and not guideline based, and a target of 140/90 is unnecessarily aggressive and could extend the infarct.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has dysarthria, a wing-beating tremor of the arms, and depression. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown rings at the corneal margins. Which pair of tests best supports the diagnosis?
options: High serum ferritin and elevated transferrin saturation
Elevated serum copper and normal ceruloplasmin
Low serum vitamin E and absent deep tendon reflexes
Low ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper
items.explanation: Wilson disease, from ATP7B mutation, reduces biliary copper excretion and incorporation into ceruloplasmin, so ceruloplasmin is typically low while urinary copper excretion is high. Corneal Kayser-Fleischer rings accompany neuropsychiatric disease in nearly all patients. Iron indices describe hemochromatosis. Normal ceruloplasmin with high copper does not fit, and vitamin E deficiency produces an ataxia that resembles Friedreich ataxia.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has 3 days of intractable hiccups and vomiting, followed by longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. She was started on interferon beta for presumed multiple sclerosis 6 months ago and has worsened. Which test explains her course?
options: Serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody only
items.explanation: Area postrema syndrome and longitudinally extensive myelitis are characteristic of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which is caused by antibodies against aquaporin-4. Interferon beta and some other multiple sclerosis agents can worsen it. Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein disease is a related diagnosis but less often presents this way. Anti-Hu suggests paraneuronal syndromes, and 14-3-3 protein supports prion disease.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has become disinhibited, makes inappropriate comments to strangers, eats only sweets, and no longer shows interest in his family. Memory testing is relatively preserved. Which imaging pattern is most likely?
options: Hippocampal atrophy with posterior cingulate hypometabolism
Hot cross bun sign in the pons
items.explanation: Disinhibition, hyperorality, loss of empathy, and relatively spared memory define behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, with frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on imaging. Hippocampal atrophy with posterior hypometabolism characterizes Alzheimer disease. The hot cross bun sign is seen in multiple system atrophy with cerebellar features, and cortical ribboning suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Imaging patterns therefore help separate the major dementia syndromes at the bedside.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has a waddling gait, calf enlargement, and difficulty rising from the floor using his hands on his legs. Creatine kinase is 18,000 U/L. Genetic analysis shows an out-of-frame deletion of exons in the dystrophin gene. Which therapy has been shown to prolong ambulation?
items.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from out-of-frame dystrophin deletions, and glucocorticoids such as prednisone or deflazacort slow the loss of strength and prolong ambulation, though they cause weight gain and growth effects. Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange treat immune neuropathies and have no role in dystrophinopathy, and coenzyme Q10 has not shown benefit for this disorder in controlled studies of muscle disease.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman reports sudden weakness of the right leg after a family conflict. When she is asked to flex her left hip against resistance, the weak right hip extends with firm downward pressure. Reflexes and imaging are normal. Which sign is demonstrated?
items.explanation: In functional leg weakness, involuntary extension of the weak hip when the opposite hip is flexed against resistance is the Hoover sign, a positive clinical sign rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. A Babinski sign is an extensor plantar response from upper motor neuron lesions. The Romberg sign tests proprioception, and the Gowers sign describes climbing the legs with the hands in proximal myopathy.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with obesity has daily headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema, and imaging is normal. Opening pressure is 36 cm of water. What is the best initial management?
items.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension with papilledema and mild to moderate visual loss is treated with acetazolamide and weight reduction, with serial visual field monitoring. Repeated lumbar punctures give only transient relief, and corticosteroids cause weight gain and are not recommended. Surgery is reserved for rapidly progressive or severe visual loss despite medical therapy, and optic nerve sheath fenestration is another option.

items.stem: A 19-year-old college student has daily irresistible sleep episodes, vivid dreams at sleep onset, and sudden bilateral knee buckling when laughing. Polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing shows a mean latency of 4 minutes and sleep onset REM periods in three naps. Which cerebrospinal fluid finding is expected?
options: Elevated protein with normal cell count
items.explanation: Daytime sleepiness with cataplexy and REM intrusion defines narcolepsy type 1, caused by loss of hypothalamic hypocretin-producing neurons. Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 is low, usually under 110 pg/mL. Oligoclonal bands point to multiple sclerosis. Raised protein with normal cells suggests an inflammatory neuropathy, and low glucose with pleocytosis suggests infection. Treatment options include sodium oxybate, pitolisant, and modafinil.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought in after weeks of vomiting from a poor diet. He has confusion, nystagmus, and a wide-based gait. An intravenous glucose infusion is available. What is the correct order of treatment?
options: Give glucose first, then thiamine after one hour
Give folate alone and watch for improvement
Give intravenous thiamine before or with the glucose
items.explanation: The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia indicates Wernicke encephalopathy, due to thiamine deficiency from malnutrition. Glucose given without thiamine can precipitate or worsen the disease by consuming remaining thiamine, so thiamine should precede or accompany it, at high parenteral doses. Folate and magnesium do not treat the deficiency, although magnesium is a cofactor and may be repleted additionally.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells per microliter has 3 weeks of headache and low-grade fever. Opening pressure at lumbar puncture is 38 cm of water, India ink is positive, and cryptococcal antigen is high. Besides antifungal therapy, which intervention reduces mortality?
options: Repeated lumbar punctures to lower pressure
Immediate start of antiretrovirals the same day
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis commonly causes raised intracranial pressure from impaired fungal clearance, and repeated lumbar punctures are the primary way to lower it, improving survival. Induction uses amphotericin with flucytosine. Acetazolamide and corticosteroids worsen outcomes in trials. Starting antiretrovirals too early increases the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome, so it is delayed for several weeks after antifungal induction.

items.stem: A 20-year-old cyclist is struck on the right temple by a fall, briefly loses consciousness, recovers fully for 2 hours, then becomes drowsy with a dilated right pupil. Computed tomography is expected to show which finding?
options: A crescent-shaped collection crossing the suture lines
Lens-shaped hyperdensity stopping at the sutures
Hyperdensity filling the basal cisterns and sulci
Multiple small hemorrhages at the gray-white junction
items.explanation: A lucid interval after temporal trauma points to epidural hematoma from rupture of the middle meningeal artery, which forms a lens-shaped collection limited by the sutures, and requires urgent evacuation. A crescentic collection crossing sutures is a subdural hematoma, usually from bridging veins. Cisternal blood is subarachnoid hemorrhage, and gray-white junction petechiae reflect diffuse axonal injury.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has 3 weeks of new temporal headache, jaw pain on chewing, fatigue, and sudden painless visual loss in the right eye. The disc is pale and swollen. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 98 mm/h. What is the best immediate action?
options: Wait for the biopsy result before any steroid
Begin low-dose aspirin and arrange outpatient review
items.explanation: Giant cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is an emergency, since the second eye can be lost within days. Steroids must start at once without waiting for biopsy, which remains informative for several weeks after treatment begins. Aspirin alone is inadequate to prevent further visual loss. Lumbar puncture does not help in a patient with elevated inflammatory markers and an ischemic optic nerve.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has dyspnea when supine, a forced vital capacity of 48 percent predicted, and daytime hypercapnia. Which intervention has been shown, besides riluzole, to prolong survival and improve quality of life?
options: Inspiratory muscle training with an incentive device
items.explanation: Noninvasive ventilation lengthens survival and preserves quality of life when respiratory muscle weakness causes orthopnea, hypercapnia, or a forced vital capacity below about 50 percent. Oxygen alone can suppress ventilatory drive in a hypercapnic patient and worsen carbon dioxide retention. Prophylactic tracheostomy is not recommended before failure of noninvasive support. Muscle training has no proven survival benefit in motor neuron disease.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with prolonged episodes of shaking lasting 8 minutes has her eyes tightly closed throughout, then recalls the event afterward. Hospital staff note no tongue laceration or incontinence. Which feature most strongly favors a functional seizure rather than an epileptic seizure?
options: Sustained eye closure during the event
Absence of any warning before the event
Occurrence in a patient with a history of anxiety
items.explanation: Eyes that stay forcefully closed during a convulsive event are among the most reliable bedside signs of a functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizure, whereas eyes are usually open in epileptic seizures. Preserved memory is more variable and less specific. Seizures without warning occur in both conditions, and a psychiatric history raises the pretest probability but cannot establish the diagnosis. Video electroencephalography remains the reference standard.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man had 20 minutes of transient left monocular visual loss 5 days ago. Duplex ultrasonography and angiography show 80 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is a reasonable surgical candidate. What is the best timing of revascularization?
options: Delay surgery for 3 months to allow recovery
Medical therapy only because the event was transient
Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks of the event
items.explanation: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70 to 99 percent carries a high early risk of stroke, and the benefit of endarterectomy is greatest when surgery occurs within 2 weeks of the event. Waiting months loses much of that benefit. Medical therapy alone is inferior in severe symptomatic stenosis. Stenting of the intracranial vessels is not indicated for an extracranial carotid lesion.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with asthma has a bilateral postural hand tremor that interferes with holding a cup. It worsens when she is anxious or tired, and it runs in her family. Which drug is the best choice?
items.explanation: Essential tremor responds to propranolol or primidone. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in significant asthma because they can provoke bronchospasm, so primidone is the preferred option, started at a low dose to limit sedation. Levodopa treats the rest tremor of Parkinson disease and does not help essential tremor. Anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl are poorly tolerated in older adults and have limited benefit.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with multiple sclerosis has taken natalizumab for 3 years after prior treatment with mitoxantrone. Which baseline factor most increases his risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?
options: Presence of oligoclonal bands in cerebrospinal fluid
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk during natalizumab therapy rises with anti-JC virus antibody positivity, particularly a high index, treatment duration beyond 2 years, and prior immunosuppression. Together these factors stratify risk and guide decisions such as extended interval dosing or switching. Sex and younger age do not raise risk, and oligoclonal bands reflect intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis in multiple sclerosis and say nothing about risk.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought in after asking the same questions again and again for 5 hours, yet she stays alert and recognizes family. Examination and imaging are normal, and she cannot recall the morning's events. By 18 hours her memory is back to normal. What is the expected prognosis?
options: High risk of an ischemic stroke within one month
Progression to Alzheimer disease within 2 years
Recurrence is uncommon and the outlook is benign
items.explanation: Transient global amnesia causes sudden anterograde amnesia with preserved alertness and personal identity that resolves within 24 hours. Recurrence is uncommon and the long-term outlook is benign, with no increased stroke risk or progression to dementia. Antiepileptic drugs are not needed unless seizures are suspected, and anticoagulation or extensive vascular workup is not routinely required.

items.stem: A 4-month-old boy has symmetric hypotonia with a bell-shaped chest, tongue fasciculations, and absent reflexes, but good social engagement. Genetic testing confirms homozygous SMN1 deletion. Which factor best predicts how severe his disease will be?
options: The size of the SMN1 deletion in base pairs
The number of SMN2 gene copies
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from loss of SMN1, and the nearly identical SMN2 gene produces a small amount of functional protein. Higher SMN2 copy numbers produce more protein and a milder phenotype, which also determines the urgency of disease-modifying treatment. Deletion size does not predict severity, creatine kinase is usually normal or mildly raised, and carrier status is irrelevant to the affected child's phenotype.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman taking lithium for bipolar disorder develops coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, and unsteady gait after a week of gastroenteritis with poor intake. Her lithium level is 2.6 mEq/L. What is the best next step?
options: Continue lithium at half the dose
Start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
Stop lithium, give isotonic saline, dialysis if severe
Give activated charcoal as the primary therapy
items.explanation: Volume depletion reduces renal lithium clearance and causes toxicity, with coarse tremor, ataxia, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Management is to stop the drug, restore volume with isotonic saline, and use hemodialysis for severe neurologic signs or very high levels. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so dose reduction is inadequate. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and thiazides raise levels. Charcoal does not bind lithium.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a body mass index of 36 has daily headaches worse when lying down, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations. Examination shows bilateral papilledema with normal brain imaging and venography. Opening pressure is 36 cm of water with normal fluid composition. Which is the best initial therapy?
items.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in an obese young woman is treated with acetazolamide and weight loss, which protect vision by lowering pressure and swelling. Surgical diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration is reserved for failing or rapidly worsening vision. Corticosteroids cause weight gain and rebound problems. Serial lumbar punctures give only transient benefit and are impractical as chronic treatment.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl cannot fall asleep before 3 a.m. and cannot wake for school, but sleeps soundly for 8 hours when allowed, including on weekends and holidays. Which intervention is most effective?
options: Nightly zolpidem taken at the usual bedtime
Evening bright light exposure before bed
items.explanation: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is a circadian misalignment, not a failure of sleep quantity or quality when sleep is allowed. Treatment shifts the clock earlier with timed low-dose melatonin several hours before the desired bedtime and bright light soon after waking. Hypnotics do not realign the rhythm. Late caffeine worsens delay, and bright light in the evening pushes the rhythm later.

items.stem: A 73-year-old vegan woman has numb, tingling feet and then progressive gait unsteadiness with loss of vibration sense. She has hyperreflexia at the knees, absent ankle jerks, and a Babinski sign. Hemoglobin is low with macrocytosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical cord would most likely show which finding?
options: T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns
Hyperintensity confined to the anterior horns
Extrinsic compression by a disc osteophyte
items.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency affects the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, and also the peripheral nerves, giving mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. Imaging often shows dorsal column T2 hyperintensity, classically an inverted V on axial slices. Anterior horn involvement fits motor neuron disease, a syrinx gives dissociated sensory loss, and compression would show extrinsic cord deformation.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has bilateral foot drop, high-arched feet, and hammer toes. His father has similar findings. Nerve conduction velocities in both arms are uniformly slowed to 20 meters per second. Which genetic test has the highest yield?
options: Repeat expansion analysis of the frataxin gene
Duplication testing of the PMP22 gene
Deletion analysis of the SMN1 gene
items.explanation: A length-dependent motor and sensory neuropathy with uniform slowing of conduction below 38 meters per second in the arms indicates a demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. The most common form, type 1A, results from a duplication of PMP22, so dosage testing is the correct first step. Dystrophin affects muscle, frataxin expansion causes Friedreich ataxia, and SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy without sensory slowing.

items.stem: A 5-month-old girl has clusters of flexor spasms on awakening and has stopped smiling. Electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia, and examination reveals hypopigmented macules and a cardiac rhabdomyoma on echocardiography. Which is the preferred treatment for her seizures?
items.explanation: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia in the setting of tuberous sclerosis respond best to vigabatrin, which raises gamma-aminobutyric acid by inhibiting its breakdown. Adrenocorticotropic hormone is an alternative first-line option. Phenobarbital and carbamazepine do not treat the syndrome effectively, and carbamazepine may worsen it. Dietary therapy is a later adjunct and is not enough as sole initial treatment.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is admitted with a Hunt and Hess grade 2 subarachnoid hemorrhage, and the aneurysm is secured on day 1. Which medication is routinely given for 21 days to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia and improve outcome?
items.explanation: Nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker, improves functional outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, probably through neuroprotection rather than relief of large vessel vasospasm, and is given for 21 days. Routine seizure prophylaxis has no proven benefit and phenytoin may worsen cognitive outcome. Corticosteroids do not reduce delayed ischemia or improve recovery after this hemorrhage. Prolonged antifibrinolytic therapy increases ischemic complications.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for 12 years has repetitive tongue protrusion and lip smacking. Switching to a lower-risk agent is planned. Which drug directly treats the movements?
options: Diazepam as a daily maintenance drug
items.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia reflects dopamine receptor supersensitivity, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine reduce the movements. Anticholinergics like benztropine treat acute dystonia and parkinsonism and can worsen tardive dyskinesia. Amantadine has limited and inconsistent benefit. Benzodiazepines may mask symptoms but are not recommended for maintenance because of sedation and dependence over long-term use.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has severe vision loss in the right eye and, a month later, a longitudinally extensive myelitis spanning five vertebral segments. Brain magnetic resonance imaging is normal. She is started on interferon beta for presumed multiple sclerosis. Which result would best explain her course?
options: Positive CSF oligoclonal bands unmatched in serum
items.explanation: Optic neuritis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and a normal brain suggests neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, defined by aquaporin-4 antibody. Interferon beta and some other multiple sclerosis therapies can worsen it, so accurate diagnosis changes treatment. Oligoclonal bands favor multiple sclerosis. Sarcoidosis can cause a long myelitis but is less likely. Anti-Hu is a paraneoplastic neuronal antibody.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has 18 months of progressive difficulty reading, judging distances, and finding objects in a cluttered drawer. She cannot reach accurately for a cup, and cannot count several objects in a single glance. Memory and language are relatively spared. Which pathology is most often responsible?
options: Alzheimer disease pathology involving the occipitoparietal cortex
Vascular dementia from small subcortical infarcts
Prion disease of the frontal lobes
items.explanation: Early visuospatial failure with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and preserved memory and language is posterior cortical atrophy, a syndrome in which the underlying pathology is most often Alzheimer disease. Vascular dementia causes stepwise decline with executive slowing. Limbic encephalitis produces subacute amnesia and seizures. Prion disease progresses over weeks to months with myoclonus rather than over a year and a half.

items.stem: A girl who walked at 12 months loses purposeful hand use and speech between 12 and 24 months. She now has continuous hand wringing, acquired microcephaly, and episodes of irregular breathing with breath holding. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Regression after initially normal development, loss of purposeful hand movement, stereotyped hand wringing, deceleration of head growth, and breathing irregularity define Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene and mostly affecting girls. FMR1 expansion causes fragile X syndrome without this regression pattern. UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome with happy demeanor and ataxia. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man treated with haloperidol for 3 days becomes febrile, with lead pipe rigidity, confusion, and fluctuating blood pressure. Creatine kinase is 9,000 U/L. Reflexes are normal and there is no clonus. Which treatment is most appropriate in addition to stopping the drug?
items.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days after dopamine blockade, with severe rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, and raised creatine kinase. Treatment is drug withdrawal, aggressive supportive care, and sometimes dantrolene or bromocriptine. Cyproheptadine is used for serotonin syndrome, which develops within hours and features hyperreflexia and clonus. Reintroducing the antipsychotic is dangerous, and benzodiazepines alone are inadequate for severe disease.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has taken a combination analgesic containing caffeine and a triptan on 15 days each month for a year to treat migraine. His headaches are now nearly daily and are present on waking. What is the best management?
options: Increase the triptan frequency to every day
Add a daily opioid for breakthrough pain
Withdraw the overused drug, start a preventive
Order repeat magnetic resonance imaging and observe
items.explanation: Using triptans on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more, can produce medication overuse headache, with daily headache that improves after withdrawal. Management combines education, stopping or limiting the culprit drug, and starting a preventive such as a beta blocker, topiramate, or a calcitonin gene-related peptide antagonist. More frequent triptan use or opioids deepen the problem. Imaging adds little when examination is normal.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and tongue wasting with fluctuating weakness. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative, and pyridostigmine worsens her cramps without improving strength. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Bulbar weakness with focal muscle atrophy and poor response to cholinesterase inhibitors suggests myasthenia gravis with antibodies to muscle-specific kinase. These patients usually lack thymic hyperplasia, so thymectomy has little benefit, and cholinergic drugs often cause side effects. B cell depletion with rituximab produces durable improvement in many patients. Edrophonium is a short-acting diagnostic agent and not a maintenance therapy.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with generalized tonic-clonic seizures is stable on valproate. She plans to switch to lamotrigine to prepare for pregnancy. Which approach lowers her risk of a serious rash?
options: Start lamotrigine at the full target dose to cover the taper period
Stop valproate abruptly and start lamotrigine on the same day
Add a prophylactic glucocorticoid for the first month of therapy
Start low, titrate slowly, and taper valproate gradually
items.explanation: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its half life, so rapid titration during overlap raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Starting low and escalating slowly is the safeguard. Beginning at target dose or switching abruptly removes that protection and risks both rash and breakthrough seizures. Prophylactic steroids are not an accepted way to prevent lamotrigine rash.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man develops abrupt vertigo, a hoarse voice, and dysphagia. On examination pain and temperature sensation are lost on the right face and the left body, right Horner syndrome, and right limb ataxia, with normal strength. Which vessel is most commonly occluded?
items.explanation: This is the lateral medullary syndrome. Crossed sensory loss reflects the spinal trigeminal nucleus and the spinothalamic tract, and the Horner syndrome, dysphagia, and ataxia complete it. Although the posterior inferior cerebellar artery is often named, the vertebral artery is the vessel most often occluded. An anterior inferior cerebellar lesion adds facial paralysis and deafness. A superior cerebellar lesion spares the lower cranial nerves, and a posterior cerebral lesion causes visual field loss.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man has 6 months of dysarthria, drooling, and wing-beating tremor of the arms. His liver enzymes are mildly raised. Slit lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the corneal limbus. Which laboratory finding is expected?
options: High serum ceruloplasmin with low urinary copper
Low serum iron with high ferritin
Raised serum manganese with normal copper
Low serum ceruloplasmin with high 24-hour urinary copper
items.explanation: Hepatic and neuropsychiatric features with Kayser-Fleischer rings indicate Wilson disease, caused by ATP7B mutations that impair biliary copper excretion. Serum ceruloplasmin is typically low, urinary copper is high, and liver copper is elevated. Treatment is chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc. Disordered iron handling suggests neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Manganese toxicity gives a parkinsonian syndrome without a corneal ring.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with relapsing multiple sclerosis has received natalizumab for 30 months. He is JC virus antibody positive with a high index. Which statement best guides his treatment plan?
options: Risk rises with longer duration, prior immunosuppression, and high index
The risk is highest in the first 6 months of therapy
A negative CSF polymerase chain reaction test excludes risk in the future
Risk is unrelated to antibody status
items.explanation: Natalizumab blocks lymphocyte entry into the central nervous system, permitting JC virus reactivation. The three risk factors are positive JC antibody status, treatment beyond about 2 years, and prior immunosuppressant use, and a higher index raises risk further. Risk is low in the first year. Testing the spinal fluid only identifies established infection, not future risk. Antibody status is a central factor in risk stratification.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has urinary urgency, a slow wide-based gait with feet that seem stuck to the floor, and mild forgetfulness over 8 months. Computed tomography shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Which finding best supports a favorable response to shunting?
options: Improved gait after a high-volume lumbar puncture
Onset of dementia years before the gait problem began
items.explanation: The triad of gait disturbance, cognitive slowing, and urinary urgency with ventriculomegaly suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus. Gait improvement after a large volume tap or an extended lumbar drain predicts shunt response. Early dementia before gait change and prominent hippocampal atrophy imply Alzheimer disease as the main problem. Sensory loss with hyperreflexia suggests myelopathy or neuropathy instead.

items.stem: A 4-month-old boy has marked hypotonia, a bell-shaped chest, tongue fasciculations, and absent reflexes. He is alert and makes good eye contact. Genetic testing shows homozygous deletion of exon 7 of SMN1. Which statement about management is correct?
options: Treatment is not useful once weakness has appeared
Corticosteroids are the established disease modifying therapy
Start early because lost motor neurons are not regained
Management is supportive only until age 2 years
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from loss of SMN1 and consequent degeneration of anterior horn cells. Disease modifying treatments, namely intrathecal nusinersen, gene replacement with onasemnogene, and oral risdiplam, work best when begun early, since neurons already lost are not restored. Waiting for later onset forfeits benefit. Steroids have no role as a disease modifying drug, and supportive care alone is no longer the standard.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has sudden left leg weakness that began after a stressful event. While supine, she cannot lift the left leg on command, yet the examiner feels the left heel press firmly downward when she lifts the right leg against resistance, and her strength normalizes with distraction. Reflexes and imaging are normal. Which finding best supports functional weakness?
items.explanation: Functional neurologic disorder is diagnosed by positive findings, not by exclusion alone. The Hoover sign, in which a weak leg extends involuntarily when the contralateral leg flexes against resistance, and give-way weakness that varies with distraction, support the diagnosis. A Babinski sign, pronator drift, and spasticity reflect corticospinal tract damage and are objective organic signs. Physiotherapy with clear explanation is the treatment.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has a 2-year history of asymmetric weakness of the right hand grip and wrist extension, with cramps and visible twitching. There is no sensory loss and reflexes are normal in the affected arm. Nerve conduction studies show conduction block in the right median and ulnar motor nerves with normal sensory responses. Which treatment is most likely to help?
items.explanation: Asymmetric, pure motor weakness with persistent partial conduction block and normal sensory studies defines multifocal motor neuropathy. It responds to intravenous immunoglobulin, which is the established first line therapy. Corticosteroids are ineffective and may worsen the weakness. Riluzole offers a modest survival benefit in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis but does not treat a conduction block disorder. Plasma exchange is useful in inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy but has little benefit here.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has had focal impaired awareness seizures with a rising epigastric sensation for 6 years. Seizures persist after adequate trials of carbamazepine and then lamotrigine, each at tolerated doses. Magnetic resonance imaging shows left hippocampal sclerosis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Trial of a third antiseizure medication alone
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated antiseizure medications defines drug resistant epilepsy, after which the chance of remission with further drugs is low. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the best surgical substrate, and resection offers seizure freedom to a majority. Another drug alone delays definitive treatment. Neurostimulation is for patients who are not resective candidates. Counseling is needed but is not sufficient.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum has a progressively severe headache and a focal seizure. Venography confirms thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus, and imaging shows a small hemorrhagic venous infarct. What is the best treatment?
options: Observation until the hemorrhage has resolved fully
Intravenous thrombolysis at a standard dose
Antiplatelet therapy alone with close imaging
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation, even when a venous infarct has hemorrhagic transformation, because treatment limits clot propagation and does not meaningfully worsen outcome. Waiting leaves the clot untreated. Systemic thrombolysis is not first line. Aspirin is inadequate. Seizure control and management of raised pressure are given alongside, and warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant follows initial therapy.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has taken metoclopramide for gastroparesis for 4 years. She now has repetitive lip smacking and tongue protrusion that bother her socially. The medication cannot be stopped. Which drug class is approved for this problem?
items.explanation: Chronic exposure to a dopamine receptor blocker causes tardive dyskinesia. When the drug cannot be withdrawn, vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine reduce the movements by depleting presynaptic dopamine. Anticholinergics can worsen tardive dyskinesia while improving acute dystonia. A dopamine agonist may aggravate the movements. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not treat it.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has fever, then confusion, ataxia, and bilateral optic neuritis 10 days after a respiratory infection. Magnetic resonance imaging shows large, poorly marginated white matter lesions in the brain. Which antibody test is most useful?
options: Serum anti-voltage gated potassium channel antibody
items.explanation: A monophasic encephalopathy with optic neuritis and large, fluffy lesions after infection is the pattern of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies are frequent in children with this syndrome or relapsing optic neuritis. Aquaporin-4 antibody is rare in young children. The 14-3-3 protein supports prion disease. Potassium channel antibodies cause limbic encephalitis in adults.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has fluctuating alertness, well-formed visual hallucinations of children in his home, and mild parkinsonism. He becomes rigid and stuporous after receiving haloperidol for agitation. Which drug is most appropriate for his cognitive and psychiatric symptoms?
items.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies shows fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism, together with severe sensitivity to dopamine blocking antipsychotics. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine reduce hallucinations and improve cognition, and are first line. Risperidone carries the same sensitivity risk as haloperidol. Memantine has weaker evidence. Benzodiazepines can worsen confusion and fall risk in this population.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has frequent falls, calf enlargement, and a Gowers maneuver. Creatine kinase is 18,000 U/L. Genetic testing reveals an out-of-frame deletion in the dystrophin gene. Which long-term medication slows loss of ambulation?
items.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy comes from out-of-frame dystrophin mutations. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisone or deflazacort, prolong ambulation, preserve respiratory and cardiac function, and reduce scoliosis, and are the standard of care. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, pyridostigmine treats myasthenic syndromes by increasing acetylcholine, and immunoglobulin is for immune neuropathies, none of which alters the course of dystrophy.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has 10 years of slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, tongue fasciculations, perioral twitching, and enlarged breasts. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated and sensory nerve action potentials are reduced. Which genetic abnormality explains this presentation?
options: Homozygous deletion of the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5
GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72
CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene
Missense mutation in the SOD1 gene on chromosome 21
items.explanation: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) arises from a CAG expansion in the androgen receptor gene. Clues are bulbar and perioral fasciculations, gynecomastia from partial androgen insensitivity, and a sensory neuronopathy. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, usually in childhood. C9orf72 and SOD1 mutations cause familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which progresses faster and has upper motor neuron signs.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman is still seizing 6 minutes after receiving adequate intravenous lorazepam in the emergency department. Her airway is protected. Which is the best next medication?
options: Intravenous phenobarbital as the only agent
Intravenous levetiracetam at 60 mg/kg up to 4500 mg
Oral topiramate through a nasogastric tube
Repeat lorazepam up to a total of six doses
items.explanation: For established status epilepticus, a second therapy phase should follow an initial benzodiazepine without delay. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate showed similar efficacy as second line agents, and levetiracetam is easy to give with few interactions. Phenobarbital is an alternative but not the first choice. Enteral topiramate is too slow and unreliable. Further repeated benzodiazepine dosing adds respiratory depression without benefit.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with progressive memory decline has a lobar hemorrhage in the right parietal region. Gradient echo imaging shows multiple small peripheral microbleeds in the cortex and subcortex of both hemispheres, sparing the basal ganglia and pons. Which condition is most likely?
items.explanation: Recurrent lobar hemorrhages and strictly lobar, cortical or subcortical microbleeds in an older adult define probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy under the Boston criteria. Hypertensive vasculopathy favors deep structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum. CADASIL causes migraine, lacunar strokes, and white matter changes in younger people. Cavernous malformations are usually few and show a popcorn appearance.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has 2 years of slowness and stiffness, with minimal benefit from carbidopa-levodopa. He faints on standing, has urinary retention, and snores with stridor at night. Examination shows jerky postural tremor and mild gait ataxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, early and severe autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, and laryngeal stridor points to multiple system atrophy. Parkinson disease responds well to levodopa and has later autonomic features. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes early falls and loss of vertical gaze, and corticobasal syndrome causes asymmetric apraxia and cortical sensory loss. Neither typically causes marked early orthostatic hypotension.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis starts fingolimod. Which monitoring is required with the first dose?
options: A baseline liver biopsy before dosing
Lumbar puncture one week after the first dose
Serum JC virus antibody before each monthly dose
Six hours of observation with heart rate checks
items.explanation: Fingolimod, a sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor modulator, can cause transient bradycardia and atrioventricular block after the first dose, so observation with serial heart rate and pressure checks is required, along with a baseline electrocardiogram. Later monitoring includes ophthalmologic review for macular edema and tests for infection and liver function. A liver biopsy and a lumbar puncture are not routine. JC antibody testing is related to natalizumab.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with early Alzheimer disease begins an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody infusion. Which monitoring is specifically required?
options: Serial magnetic resonance imaging for ARIA
items.explanation: Anti-amyloid antibodies such as lecanemab and donanemab can cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, either edema or microhemorrhage, which are usually asymptomatic but occasionally serious. Scheduled magnetic resonance imaging early in treatment is required, and risk is higher in apolipoprotein E e4 homozygotes. Bone density, drug level checks, and routine electroencephalography are not part of the monitoring protocol.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has difficulty rising from a chair and gripping a bottle cap. Examination shows weak finger flexors and atrophy of the quadriceps, with mild dysphagia. Creatine kinase is 400 U/L. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation and rimmed vacuoles. A 3-month course of high dose prednisone produced no improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Finger flexor and quadriceps weakness in an older man, with rimmed vacuoles and endomysial infiltrates, is typical of sporadic inclusion body myositis. It is notably resistant to immunosuppression. Polymyositis causes proximal weakness that improves with steroids. Dermatomyositis has skin findings and perifascicular atrophy. Necrotizing myopathy shows very high creatine kinase with fiber necrosis and little inflammation, and it usually responds to treatment.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with focal seizures is started on carbamazepine. Three weeks later he is lethargic and mildly confused. His sodium is 121 mmol/L and he is euvolemic with concentrated urine. What is the mechanism of this adverse effect?
options: Inhibition of renal sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
Reduced aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex
Enhanced antidiuretic hormone action on the kidney
Direct osmotic diuresis through glucose loss
items.explanation: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine cause a syndrome resembling inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, with water retention, euvolemic hyponatremia, and concentrated urine. Older adults are at higher risk. The drug does not act like a loop diuretic, and it does not suppress aldosterone in a way that produces significant salt wasting. An osmotic diuresis from glucose would give hypovolemia, not a euvolemic picture.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman taking warfarin has sudden right hemiparesis and vomiting. Computed tomography shows a 30 mL left basal ganglia hemorrhage. Her INR is 3.8 and her blood pressure is 192/104 mm Hg. Which is the best immediate management?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K
Oral vitamin K only, with repeat INR the next day
items.explanation: Warfarin related intracerebral hemorrhage needs rapid and complete reversal because hematoma expansion occurs in the first hours. Prothrombin complex concentrate corrects the INR faster than plasma and with less volume, and vitamin K sustains the effect. Plasma alone is slow. Oral vitamin K alone acts too late. Platelet transfusion does not reverse a vitamin K antagonist. Systolic pressure should also be lowered promptly.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has 3 weeks of emotional lability, clumsiness, and random, flowing movements of the face and limbs that disappear in sleep. She had a sore throat 2 months ago. Which cardiac evaluation is most important?
options: Echocardiography to look for rheumatic valvulitis
items.explanation: Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever and follows group A streptococcal infection after a long latency. Carditis coexists in many patients, so echocardiography is essential, and penicillin prophylaxis follows. Atrial fibrillation, coronary disease, and exercise related cardiomyopathy are not features of this syndrome. Symptomatic therapy with valproate or a dopamine blocker is optional in disabling cases.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has painful loss of vision in the left eye over 4 days, with a relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal optic disc. Brain magnetic resonance imaging shows three periventricular T2 lesions. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Oral prednisone alone is the preferred regimen
Steroids improve final acuity and prevent later multiple sclerosis
No treatment is needed because brain lesions predict full recovery
Methylprednisolone speeds recovery but not final acuity
items.explanation: In the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, intravenous methylprednisolone speeded visual recovery, but long term acuity was the same as in untreated patients, and oral prednisone alone raised the recurrence rate. Brain lesions on magnetic resonance imaging identify a high risk of multiple sclerosis and favor starting disease modifying therapy, though steroids do not reduce that risk. Recovery is usually good but is accelerated by treatment.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes develops severe unilateral thigh pain, followed over weeks by quadriceps weakness and 10 kg weight loss. Examination shows an absent knee jerk on that side. Electromyography shows denervation in lumbosacral paraspinal and thigh muscles. Which diagnosis fits best?
items.explanation: Painful, subacute proximal leg weakness with weight loss in a diabetic patient suggests diabetic amyotrophy, an ischemic microvasculitic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy. Denervation of the paraspinal muscles shows the lesion lies proximal to a single nerve. Length dependent polyneuropathy is symmetric and distal. A femoral neuropathy would spare paraspinals. A single root compression would not explain multilevel involvement or marked weight loss.

items.stem: A 5-month-old girl has clusters of brief flexor spasms on waking and has stopped smiling. Electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia. Magnetic resonance imaging is normal. Which initial treatment is recommended?
items.explanation: Epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia and developmental regression define infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, an emergency because delay worsens developmental outcome. First line therapy is hormonal treatment with corticotropin or high dose prednisolone, with vigabatrin as the choice when tuberous sclerosis is present. Phenytoin and carbamazepine are ineffective and may aggravate spasms. Ethosuximide treats absence seizures. Early treatment protects development.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of transient left monocular visual loss 4 days ago. Ultrasound and CT angiography show 75 percent stenosis at the origin of the left internal carotid artery. He is neurologically normal and a good surgical candidate. What is the best recommendation?
options: Endarterectomy within 2 weeks plus medical therapy
Elective endarterectomy delayed for 3 months after the event
Medical therapy alone since his symptoms have resolved
Carotid stenting without dual antiplatelet therapy
items.explanation: Symptomatic stenosis of 70 percent or more benefits clearly from revascularization, and the benefit is greatest when surgery occurs within about 2 weeks, because early recurrence risk is highest. Waiting months forfeits that benefit. Transient retinal ischemia counts as a symptomatic event, so medical therapy alone is inadequate. Stenting needs dual antiplatelet therapy to prevent stent thrombosis, so omitting it is unsafe.

items.stem: A 41-year-old violinist has cramping and twisting of the left hand only while playing, with normal examination at rest and during other tasks. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Task specific focal dystonia, such as musician's dystonia or writer's cramp, is best treated with botulinum toxin into the overactive muscles, which provides reliable benefit for several months. Oral agents like baclofen and trihexyphenidyl are less effective and limited by adverse effects. Levodopa helps dopa responsive dystonia, which starts in childhood with diurnal variation. Propranolol treats performance anxiety tremor, not dystonia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has progressive exertional dyspnea, difficulty climbing stairs, and morning headaches. Examination shows proximal weakness and a forced vital capacity that falls 25 percent when supine. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and muscle biopsy shows vacuoles with glycogen accumulation. Which treatment targets the underlying defect?
options: Enzyme replacement with recombinant alglucosidase alfa
items.explanation: Proximal weakness with early respiratory failure and a large supine drop in vital capacity indicates late onset Pompe disease, a deficiency of acid alpha glucosidase causing lysosomal glycogen storage. Recombinant enzyme replacement slows decline and stabilizes respiratory function. Coenzyme Q10 and carnitine help primary deficiency states but not glycogen storage. Prednisone would not correct the enzyme defect and may worsen weakness.
